messages.body_plain:
Hi Christina,

you can (right now) use a few (say 1-50) SNPs in a GenomicSEM model as instrumental variables (in the same sense SNPs are used as instrumental variables in mendelian randomization). The reason a PRS (like  a PRS based on (almost) all SNPs) won't work is that all that information thats present in the summary statistics is already used in the model, its used to estimate the heritability, and the genetic covariance. So in effect you would be double counting them if you add a PRS.

If your PRS is a composite of a few SNPs that are not in LD you probably could add them to the model as a score, but I would favor adding them individually. In terms of what sumstats to use, the most important criteria is the following:

GenomicSEM work regardless of sample overlap between the GWASes, BUT using a SNP as instrument in genomicSEM you have to adhere to the laws of mendelian randomization, that is you can use the effect sizes in the GWAS IF the exposure and outcome GWAS do not have sample overlap, or if the exposure and outcome GWAS overlap you need to use an external GWAS to select which SNPS will serve as instruments.

Hope this helps,

Best,
Michel

messages.body_plain:
Hi Nora,

Of course and thanks for sending the requested LDSC output over e-mail. I've attached an R script that lays out some of what I talk about in this response, but have also pasted it below. The genetic covariance matrix all looks reasonable in the output you sent. For the model output you sent below, the standardized estimates are quite high, including some above 1, because of the strong negative correlations between your factors. If you do the path tracing for an trait for the model output you list below, you still get a total variance of 1 (see beginning of code listed below for an example for trait 9). For a negative correlation of -.94 in the four factor model between factors 3 and 4 I would start to question whether you really need a fourth factor since it overlaps so much with Factor 3. On a separate note, one other thing to watch out for is that when you have a factor with only two indicators (e.g., Factor 2 in your four factor model, or Factor 3 in your three factor model), you need to constrain the loadings to be the same across the two in order for the model to be locally identified. An example of how to do this is in the code below for your original 3-factor model, but it involves writing the same parameter label for both loadings (e.g., F3=~a*trait8 + a*trait9).

I ran a correlated 2-factor EFA and found that it doesn't fit overly well, which I imagine is part of what also lead you to trying out the 3 and 4-factor models. I then tried specifying the 3-factor model with a cut-off of .35 from EFA factor loadings to determine which indicators load on which factors. This results in generally less factor loadings then what you specified in your 3-factor model, which helps with model convergence in this case. For Factor 3, this means that only trait 9 loads on the factor, which is perfectly acceptable. I set the residual variance of trait 9 to 0 in this case, which means Factor 3 is really just trait 9 specified as a latent factor. One of the main reasons I do this is because lavaan won't let you examine correlations between observed variables and latent variables. The model fit for this model is pretty good by conventional standards, and something I would personally think is acceptable to write-up and report. Your four factor model fits really well I think, but again I don't know that it buys you much as far as information gained. I know there's a lot here so feel free to follow-up with any questions!

-Andrew

Hi Nora,

1. You are right that std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE constraints the latent factor variances to 1. This was a recently added argument that is ultimately just a little easier to use than writing out all of the factor variances.

2. If you ran a model that included only the factor with it's 2 indicators it wouldn't converge. This is because you would be estimating the two factor loadings, and the two residual variances of the indicators (i.e., 4 free parameters), but you only have 3 degrees of freedom for this part of the covariance matrix: the 2 variances, and the covariance between the two variables. So without constraining the factor loadings to be equal you are estimating 1 too many parameters (i.e., -1 df). Since your model includes other factors/variables the model will run in this case, but results are not interpretable because it's not locally identified for the two-indicator factor without those constraints.

All good questions so let me know if anything else comes up!

-Andrew
